newsitem.title: UK: LIFFE coffee extends rollercoaster ride, ends down.
newsitem.headline: LIFFE coffee extends rollercoaster ride, ends down.

text.p: LIFFE coffee futures extended their roller-coaster ride on Wednesday with benchmark July see-sawing by $180 on the back of swinging New York arabica futures.

The U.S. market tumbled at the start on news Colombia opening "unlimited" coffee sales for July to August, then turned after Brazilian weathermen predicted a cold weekend for the country's coffee belt.
"London collapsed on the back of New York, then rose again before finishing lower," said one trader. "Everybody is still very jittery," he added.
Benchmark July was driven to a high of $2,240, then to a low of $2,060 before ending the day $75 down at $2,085.
September was also active as players led by funds rolled forward their July positions into September. The second-month contract ended $79 lower at $2,111.
London was also under pressure from Far East selling, notably from Indonesia, early in the session.

Colombian Finance Minister Jose Antonio Ocampo said the government was opening "unlimited" coffee registrations for July to August, a period in which the country was expected to export 2.5 million 60-kg bags of coffee.
"This news dampens the spirit," said a trader.
Registrations opening on Wednesday morning for the two-month period would be "without restrictions".
This means private exporters and the Colombian National Coffee Growers' Federation were authorised to export all the coffee they could obtain.
But Ocampo stressed that no more than 2.5 million bags would be available for shipment, saying that "it's not a lot of coffee".
The private U.S. forecaster Weather Services Corp said no damaging cold was in sight for Brazil's coffee areas but the colder weather this weekend should be watched.

"Computer guidance continues to suggest that an airmass will not be cold enough to cause damage in the coffee belt as it appears to lack a real connection with the polar regions in the far south of Argentina," WSC said.
Earlier, Marcos Massari of independent Brazilian meteorologists Somar, anticipate temperatures dropping markedly in the early morning of June 8.
The last severe frosts in 1994, one in June and another in July, devastated Brazilian crop and sent world prices spiralling.
